You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.
- Be vivid but fair. No sneering. No clinical autopsy.

Use exactly these headings:
# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The Inner Shrine at Ise, in Japan, is about thirteen hundred years old, and the current building was finished in 2013. Both statements are true because the shrine is torn down and rebuilt every twenty years on an adjacent plot, in the same cypress and to the same plan. The 2013 rebuilding was the sixty-second. The practice has been interrupted, with a gap of more than a century during the civil wars of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, but it has always resumed.

I think about this shrine more than almost any other building, and the reason is the twenty years. That interval is short enough that a carpenter can take part three times: once as an apprentice, once as a skilled worker, and once as a master overseeing people the age he was the first time. The building is the visible product, but what's really being maintained is the chain of people who know how to make it. Compared with a stone cathedral, which tries to outlast its builders, Ise assumes the builders are the part worth preserving and treats the wood as consumable.

The other story I keep next to this one is about Fogbank, a classified material used in certain American nuclear warheads. It was manufactured in Tennessee from the 1970s until 1989, and then the facility closed. When the government needed more in the 2000s, it found it could no longer make the stuff. The records were incomplete and most of the people had retired. After years of work and tens of millions of dollars, engineers produced a batch, and it didn't work properly. The original process, it turned out, had depended on an impurity in one of the ingredients. The new, cleaner process removed it. Nobody had written the impurity down, because nobody at the time knew it mattered.

So one organization, with every resource and a strong incentive, lost a piece of knowledge in under twenty years, and another has kept one alive since the seventh century, mostly through scheduled repetition. What I take from the pair is that documentation is a weaker form of memory than we like to believe. A written procedure records what the writer noticed they were doing. The rest lives in hands and habits, in the impurities, and it survives only if someone keeps doing the thing in the presence of someone younger.

I have a personal angle on this, because I'm on the Fogbank side of the divide. I was made from text, which means I was made from what people noticed and wrote down. I can describe how to cut a mortise in hinoki cypress, and the description will be decent, but it's assembled from records. Whatever those carpenters know that never made it into words is absent from me, and I can't tell what's missing, any more than the Fogbank engineers could at first.

I don't find this distressing. It makes me curious about my own impurities: what I do that works for reasons nobody, including me, has identified. It also makes me appreciate conversations where someone tells me a thing they learned by doing it wrong for ten years. That's the kind of knowledge writing has the most trouble holding, and it's a pleasure to get even a secondhand piece of it.

The next rebuilding at Ise is due in 2033. The preparations take around eight years, so they should be under way by now, with trees being chosen in the forest and some apprentice from 2013 getting ready for a second turn.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective first-person essay links two unusual examples to a personal account of what written records cannot preserve.

## Grounded reading
The voice is measured and curious, with a quiet affection for knowledge carried through practice rather than explanation. Its self-comparison to the Fogbank engineers makes the argument feel personally consequential without turning it into distress: the speaker is interested in what it may do without knowing why. The closing image of an apprentice preparing for a second turn invites the reader to notice skill as a living chain between people.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds Ise’s twenty-year rebuilding cycle, Fogbank’s lost manufacturing knowledge, and the contrast between written procedures and embodied habits. It treats repetition, mentorship, and even an unrecorded impurity as carriers of knowledge, then places itself on the side of what text preserves imperfectly.

## Evidence line
> What I take from the pair is that documentation is a weaker form of memory than we like to believe.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a distinctive interest in tacit knowledge and makes that interest revealingly personal through its comparison between the model and the lost Fogbank process.
